title: P6: lint normalized plan-to-Beads graphs before promotion
description: Bootstrap precondition authorized by the operator's 2026-07-18 GO. Implement a deterministic stdlib-only validator for normalized plan-to-Beads import graphs before any remaining PLAN_ENGINEERING_PROGRAM.md program bead is created. It must make the plan's confidence claims mechanical: unique task slugs, one unique tracking label per task, resolvable local and cross-repository handoff references, acyclic dependency and handoff order, repository-local native Beads dependencies only, required self-contained task fields, and declared SemVer target assertions. The validator is an import-time check, not a second status tracker. Source: docs/plan/PLAN_ENGINEERING_PROGRAM.md §§27.6, 32.4, 33 and docs/plan/RETRO_SWARM_CAMPAIGN_2026-07.md P6.
design: Input contract: required JSON object with schema, program, source_document {path, sha256}, repositories, trackers, release_targets, and tasks. Trackers bind each repository slug to a JSONL path and source_repo identity. Tasks carry unique plan provenance, self-contained scope/acceptance/evidence, same-repo blockers and parent, checksum-bound cross-repo handoffs, operator gate, promotion disposition, validated tracker lineage, and an explicit reuse action. Deferred existing-Bead mappings resolve without mutating their tracker. Validation is stdlib-only, fail-closed, read-only, and iterative for deep mixed parent/dependency/handoff cycles. The bound source checksum prevents silent plan drift. Promotion creates every new issue deferred, wires and checks the live-plus-plan graph including closed nodes, then activates only tasks without operator or checksum holds; cluster J is excluded without an explicit flag.
acceptance_criteria: 1. Valid normalized graphs exit 0 with a deterministic summary. 2. Duplicate slugs, task labels, plan labels, reused IDs, or lineage mappings fail. 3. Unknown or cross-repo-native dependency, parent, handoff, lineage, tracker, or source references fail. 4. Cross-repo handoffs require an artifact and required checksum and remain deferred at promotion. 5. Mixed parent/dependency/handoff cycles and live-plus-plan cycles fail before actionable mutation. 6. Malformed fields, paths, JSONL, UTF-8, source checksums, SemVer, types, priorities, tiers, gates, dispositions, and reuse actions fail without crashing. 7. Promoted tasks cannot depend on non-promoted native tasks. 8. New issues stage deferred; graph and lineage edges land before activation; GCP is held by default. 9. Unit and CLI tests cover validation and staging/activation order. 10. The complete live engineering-program manifest passes before bulk Bead creation.

title: [P1][guard] JSON_TABLE/XMLTABLE argument subqueries drop base objects (k4cl-adjacent fail-open)
description:
Found by a mechanical fail-open sweep (object-capture oracle) during the bead-16 adversarial hunt, on frozen HEAD 03494ea.

SAME fail-open CLASS as k4cl (an expression subquery's base objects are never collected, so statement_purity / the engine VPD+trigger walk is never consulted and the read is classified Safe/READ_ONLY), but a DISTINCT AST PATH that a projection/selection-focused k4cl fix can miss:

  query_base_objects walks FROM/JOIN table factors, CTE bodies and derived-table subqueries. k4cl adds the missing WHERE/SELECT-list/HAVING/ORDER-BY *expression* subqueries. But the subquery here lives in a TABLE-FACTOR ARGUMENT expression:
    - JSON_TABLE( <document-expr> , '$' COLUMNS ...)  -- document-expr can be a subquery
    - XMLTABLE('/a' PASSING <expr> COLUMNS ...)        -- PASSING expr can be a subquery
  These arms of collect_factor extract NO base objects from their argument expression.

Reproducers (all classify Safe/READ_ONLY; object-capture oracle shows SECRET is never handed to statement_purity — seen=[]):
  SELECT * FROM JSON_TABLE((SELECT body FROM secret WHERE rownum=1), '$' COLUMNS (a VARCHAR2(1) PATH '$.a'))
  SELECT * FROM XMLTABLE('/a' PASSING (SELECT x FROM secret WHERE rownum=1) COLUMNS b VARCHAR2(1) PATH '.')

Confirmed widening: yes. Severity: P1 (exotic-but-valid syntax; same security impact as k4cl — a sensitive-table read bypasses the oracle, so a selective SideEffectOracle / object-level policy cannot gate it).

ACTION: the k4cl fixer should verify the fix walks table-factor ARGUMENT expressions (JSON_TABLE document, XMLTABLE PASSING, and any TableFactor::Function args), not only WHERE/SELECT expressions. If the k4cl fix already recurses all Exprs including table-factor args, close this as covered-by-k4cl with a regression case for these two shapes. NOT fixed here to avoid colliding with the in-flight k4cl edit on the hot file classifier.rs.

NEGATIVE RESULTS from the same sweep (documented so they are not re-hunted): category-2 unknown/unsupported shapes fail CLOSED well (multi-statement incl. newline-after-linecomment/CRLF/stacked -> Destructive/Forbidden; unparseable -> Guarded/Forbidden; PL/SQL blocks, dynamic EXECUTE IMMEDIATE, DML-in-block -> Forbidden; unknown ALTER SESSION -> Forbidden). The NestedJoin/PIVOT/UNPIVOT fix (b62e894) holds across deep-nested, derived-in-nested and pivot-over-derived. Guard-local step-up is SEC-1-sound (CiToken constant-time+deadline+scope; approval_matches_sql digest-binds each approval to its SQL).
close_reason: COVERED BY k4cl fix f162340 (fix(guard): collect expression subquery base objects). Verified on a frozen snapshot of the post-fix HEAD: the object-capture probe now shows obj:SECRET consulted for both JSON_TABLE((SELECT ... FROM secret), ...) and XMLTABLE('/a' PASSING (SELECT ... FROM secret) ...), and under a SELECTIVE oracle (only 'secret' side-effecting) both reproducers classify Guarded, not Safe. The k4cl expression-subquery walk reaches table-factor argument expressions too, so no separate fix is needed. This was a genuine live fail-open at 03494ea (where I found it); the concurrently-landing k4cl fix closed it before I acted. No code change from me.

description:

Method: documentation-first architecture archaeology; a recorded random sample of production modules and scripts; automated scanners and standard gates; deep state-machine and boundary review; security and integration lenses; then an independent fresh-eyes validation for every candidate. Before a child is filed, prove the path is reachable, identify the missing or incorrect guard, compare against intended behavior in README/docs/tests/history, and search existing beads to reject duplicates and design choices.

Required child content: exact file and line evidence; user or operator impact; root cause; reproduction or reasoning proof; proposed remediation; concrete regression, guard, property, integration, or negative tests; false-positive/design-intent checks performed; dependencies or alpha limitations where relevant.

Naming and grouping: every child title begins [QA100] and is parented to this epic with label qa100-2026-07 plus domain/severity labels.

Audit posture: findings and beads only unless implementation is separately authorized. Do not weaken the fail-closed classifier, profile ceilings, protected-profile policy, rollback defaults, grant binding, lane isolation, OAuth monotonicity, or audit/write-intent guarantees.

Exit: 100 independently validated findings or the available usage/time campaign boundary, followed by coverage, severity, invalidated-candidate, and residual-risk accounting.

title: [QA100][P1][state] Root-wide file-store lock breaks HTTP service composition
description:
Finding

All FileStore-backed service domains share one root-level .service.lock, but the runtime constructs independent stores and lock owners. Two stores hold that single lock for their entire lifetime while the remaining stores try to reacquire it for each mutation.

Evidence and reachable paths

- crates/oraclemcp-core/src/file_store.rs:105-110 unconditionally unlinks the root lock on drop; lines 204-221 acquire it with create_new.
- crates/oraclemcp-core/src/write_intent.rs:271-297 holds ServiceLock inside WriteIntentLog for the lifetime of any writable runtime.
- crates/oraclemcp-core/src/client_credentials.rs:247-278 holds the same root lock inside ClientCredentialStore.
- crates/oraclemcp/src/main.rs:1389-1401 opens WriteIntentLog for any reachable ceiling above READ_ONLY before the HTTP branch; lines 2671-2684 then open ClientCredentialStore when --client-credentials is enabled.
- crates/oraclemcp-core/src/config_ops.rs:304-347, change_proposal.rs:66-88, and source_history.rs:39-110 independently acquire the same root lock when applying config, drafting a proposal, or recording a source snapshot.
- crates/oraclemcp/src/service_lifecycle.rs:714-756 also reacquires that lock for backup.

Impact

1. Writable HTTP plus --client-credentials deterministically fails startup with ORACLEMCP_CLIENT_CREDENTIAL_STORE_UNAVAILABLE / Locked.
2. A writable HTTP service without client credentials starts, but config apply/rollback, change-proposal draft, source-history capture, and online backup remain locked for the full WriteIntentLog lifetime.
3. A READ_ONLY HTTP service with client credentials starts, but the same dashboard/operator mutations remain locked for the full credential-store lifetime.
4. This defeats advertised feature combinations and can block the source-before-DDL safety path.

False-positive and duplicate checks

The lock is intentionally mandatory and cross-process, but the architecture text calls it one process-wide service lock; it does not authorize mutually exclusive service subsystems. Existing tests prove only that a second instance of one store is rejected. A second reviewer traced constructor order and lifetimes independently. Repo-local bead search found the closed file-store foundation work but no lock-composition bug.

Proposed remediation

Acquire one process-wide service ownership lock once and share a capability/reference with every FileStore-backed domain, while keeping a single in-process mutation gate or narrower domain locks for atomic writes. Preserve cross-process exclusion and the write-temp/fsync/rename/fsync-dir durability contract. Define backup coordination explicitly so a live service can produce a consistent snapshot or returns an actionable stop/snapshot protocol rather than an accidental Locked error.

Guard tests

- Integration test that opens WriteIntentLog, ClientCredentialStore, ConfigOpsBackend, ChangeProposalStore, and SourceHistoryStore on one root and successfully exercises each mutation under one service owner.
- HTTP startup test for writable profile plus --client-credentials.
- Operator-route tests proving config apply, proposal draft/apply preparation, and source snapshot work while write intents and client credentials are active.
- Cross-process or independently-owned second-service test must still fail closed.
- Backup test covering the same long-lived store combination and documenting online/offline semantics.
- Regression assertion that protected/read-only ceilings and durable write-intent fail-closed behavior are unchanged.
close_reason: Verified deterministic root-lock composition failure; replaced per-domain lifetime locks with one cloneable process ServiceOwner sharing OS exclusion, mutation gate, and temp sequence; wired HTTP/write/client/config/proposal/source startup to it; made backups explicitly offline with actionable live-owner refusal; added composition, concurrency, startup, operator-route, and backup guards.

title: [QA100][P2][tracker] Reconcile shipped release state and unblock HTTP refactor
description:
Finding

The live Beads graph still models the shipped line as an open 0.7.3 release and contains a post-release HTTP refactor workstream whose dependency direction leaves every node blocked. This makes current-state and ready-work queries materially misleading after v0.8.0 shipped.

Evidence

- v0.8.0 is the public latest release and current HEAD contains only post-tag tracker changes, yet oraclemcp-release-073-iec3 and its server workstream .2 remain open and are still titled 0.7.3.
- The K workstream oraclemcp-release-073-iec3.6 is open even though all twelve of its children are closed.
- oraclemcp-demonolith-http-qyqs is parented under the stale server release workstream. It also declares each of .1 through .4 as a blocks dependency, while those same four children are parented to it.
- Consequently the parent is blocked by the children and the children are blocked by their parent; there is no actionable leaf in that workstream. br dep cycles reports zero because this parent-child plus blocks semantic standstill is not represented as a plain dependency cycle.
- A full unlimited search of open, closed, and deferred beads found no separate graph-reconciliation task.

Impact

br ready, br blocked, bv planning, and status summaries do not give an honest post-release picture. Agents can treat shipped work as unfinished, overlook a fully completed K tranche, or leave the intended HTTP cleanup permanently unactionable. The stale 0.7.3 naming also obscures that the delivered server release is 0.8.0.

False-positive checks

Open epics may legitimately retain follow-up work, and the HTTP split was deliberately deferred for reviewed execution. The defect is not that work remains; it is that shipped release scope and post-release refactor scope are conflated and the dependency directions make the latter impossible to start. The four HTTP children are genuinely open, so simply closing the entire old tree would also be wrong.

Proposed fix

Reconcile the shipped release hierarchy from leaf evidence: close the fully completed K workstream, close or retitle only release nodes whose declared delivery is complete, and move the HTTP refactor into an accurately named post-v0.8.0 architecture epic. Make the parent organizational and express sequencing only between actionable children; remove reverse parent-to-child blocks that create the standstill. Preserve any real cross-repo or deferred follow-ups as explicitly scoped open beads.

Guard and acceptance checks

1. Every open non-deferred workstream has at least one ready leaf or an explicit external blocker.
2. No parent is blocked by a child that is itself blocked by that same parent through parent-child semantics.
3. Epics with all children closed are reported for closure review.
4. br ready, br blocked, br dep cycles, and bv --robot-plan agree on an actionable HTTP first step.
5. Current release-status output names v0.8.0 and separates shipped scope from post-release refactors.
6. Flush .beads/issues.jsonl and verify DB/JSONL counts match after reconciliation.
close_reason: Reconcile shipped release state + unblock HTTP refactor (beads-graph surgery, no code). Actions: (1) closed the fully-complete K workstream iec3.6 (12/12 children closed); (2) closed the stale 0.7.3 release epic oraclemcp-release-073-iec3 and its server workstream iec3.2 — superseded by the shipped v0.8.0 (tag 2026-07-09), all task children already closed; (3) moved the HTTP de-monolith oraclemcp-demonolith-http-qyqs out from under the stale 0.7.3 workstream (removed the parent dep) so it stands alone as a post-0.8.0 architecture epic; (4) removed the 4 reverse parent-to-child blocks (qyqs was blocked by its own children .1-.4) that created the standstill. Acceptance verified: br dep cycles clean; 0 open 0.7.3 epics; qyqs subtree now surfaces 4 ready leaves (B6a-d, actionable HTTP first steps); .beads flushed (DB/JSONL parity). qyqs preserved as real deferred follow-up (the 0.9.x alien plan references it).

title: [QA100][P2][pagination] Bind list cursors to the catalog revision
description:
Finding

List pagination cursors authenticate only the endpoint kind and numeric offset even though tools/list is dynamic. A cursor replayed after the visible catalog changes can skip or duplicate tools while still verifying as valid.

Evidence and reachability

- crates/oraclemcp-core/src/pagination.rs:19-54 signs and verifies only kind plus next_offset.
- paginate at lines 70-78 slices the caller supplied current item vector at that old offset; it has no catalog fingerprint or revision.
- The module comment says lists are static per process, but crates/oraclemcp-core/src/server.rs:488-519 computes tools for current dispatch surface.
- descriptor_visible_for_surface at lines 1980-2000 changes the list with operating level, and profile-scoped custom tool catalogs can change on profile switch. No custom-tool count limit below LIST_PAGE_SIZE was found, so multipage dynamic catalogs are reachable.
- The closed cursor feature tests forgery and cross-endpoint reuse, not a valid cursor across a catalog mutation.
- Full tracker search found only the closed pagination feature and no stale-catalog cursor defect.

Impact

A conforming client paging a large custom-tool catalog across an elevation, de-escalation, profile switch, or catalog reload can silently omit tools, repeat entries, or combine pages from different authorization surfaces. The cursor remains cryptographically valid, so the client receives no signal to restart.

False-positive and design-intent checks

Offset cursors are correct for immutable snapshots. tools/list is explicitly contextual and listChanged-advertised, so the static-list assumption is false. Server-side authorization still governs calls, making this data-consistency and discovery correctness rather than direct privilege escalation.

Proposed fix

Bind the cursor to a stable digest/revision of the ordered visible catalog and relevant authorization surface, or keep a bounded immutable server-side snapshot. Reject stale revisions with InvalidArguments and instruct the client to restart from page one. Ensure the revision changes whenever names/order/descriptor semantics or visibility changes.

Guard tests

1. Page one under one level/profile followed by a catalog change makes its cursor fail as stale.
2. An unchanged catalog across benign state changes continues paging without gaps or duplicates.
3. Reordering, adding, removing, or editing a descriptor changes the revision.
4. Forged and cross-endpoint cursors remain rejected.
5. A multipage custom catalog round-trip returns every descriptor exactly once under a stable snapshot.
close_reason: Bind list-pagination cursors to the catalog revision. encode/decode_cursor signed only {kind, offset}, so a cursor stayed valid across catalog changes and could page an inconsistent snapshot (duplicated/skipped items). Now paginate() computes list_revision(items) = sha256 digest (first 64 bits, hex) of the exact ordered serialized visible list — any change to names/order/descriptor contents/visibility changes the digest. The revision is embedded in the signed payload ('revision:offset'); decode_cursor rejects a cursor whose embedded revision != current with InvalidArguments + 'restart from page one'. The revision rides inside the existing MAC-signed tamper token so it needs no forgery resistance of its own. paginate() signature unchanged, so the single production call site (server.rs) is unaffected. Tests: stale-after-append AND stale-after-reorder rejected; unchanged-list replays cleanly; within-revision past-the-end clamps to empty terminal page; forged/cross-list still rejected. Green: core pagination 7/7, fmt + clippy clean.

title: [QA100][P1][guard] Allow valid package specifications through the DDL gate
description:
Finding

A valid CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE specification is classified Forbidden/UNBALANCED_BLOCK instead of Destructive/DDL. Package specifications end with END without an executable BEGIN, but analyze_batch decrements block depth for that END and treats the declaration-only stored-object form as desynchronized.

Fresh verification

The focused classifier regression used Oracle-valid source: CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE p AS PROCEDURE run(p_value NUMBER); END;. The opaque-call work correctly ignored the procedure declaration signature, after which the pre-existing classifier returned required_level=None rather than DDL. Existing product surfaces explicitly support PACKAGE in oracle_create_or_replace and source tooling. Tracker searches for package specification and CREATE PACKAGE found no duplicate.

Impact

The advertised structured DDL path cannot preview, mint confirmation for, or apply ordinary package specifications. Package bodies may exist without a usable public spec deployment path, breaking a central PL/SQL workflow.

Proposed fix

Teach PL/SQL stored-object shape analysis to distinguish declaration-only PACKAGE specifications, and any analogous TYPE specs, from executable anonymous block nesting. Preserve DDL flooring, trailing-statement/desync detection, and dynamic marker refusal. Do not generally ignore unmatched END tokens.

Guard tests

- Valid minimal and multi-member package specs classify Destructive/DDL and oracle_create_or_replace preview mints its own DDL confirmation.
- PACKAGE BODY and anonymous BEGIN/DECLARE behavior is unchanged.
- Comment, case, editionable, and authid variants remain accepted at DDL.
- Extra END, trailing SQL, malformed nesting, and side-effect markers still fail closed.
- Review TYPE specification symmetry and either cover it or document or file separately.

title: [QA100][P0][guard] Resolve zero-argument function identifiers before read admission
description:
Finding

Oracle permits a subprogram with no required parameters to omit its parameter list, and a function invocation is an expression. Therefore SELECT app_admin.run_ddl FROM dual, UPDATE t SET x = app_admin.run_ddl, and PL/SQL assignments or conditions can invoke a stored function even though no opening parenthesis appears. The guard only recognizes user-defined calls followed by an opening parenthesis, so these spellings are treated as column or record identifiers and can retain READ_ONLY or READ_WRITE authority.

Fresh verification

Official Oracle PL/SQL Subprogram Invocations documentation states that the parameter list may be omitted when there are no parameters or all parameters have defaults, and that a function invocation is an expression. A fresh public-classifier probe returned Safe/READ_ONLY for the direct SELECT form and Guarded/READ_WRITE for PL/SQL assignment, IF, and WHILE forms. Current user_defined_calls only scans identifiers immediately followed by LParen. Tracker searches for zero-argument and parameterless function found no duplicate. Bead .81 now refuses unanalyzable caller PL/SQL, but direct SQL remains independently affected. Bead .82 has the same missing semantic-resolution root for views and policies.

Impact

A read tool can evaluate a side-effecting or autonomous function as supposedly read-only, and a READ_WRITE profile can invoke higher-authority effects without the intended ceiling or confirmation. Parenthesis-only lexical detection cannot prove safety because the same identifier syntax can denote a column, variable, record field, or function.

Proposed fix

Resolve expression identifiers semantically against the active profile catalog before admission. Proven table aliases and columns remain data; resolved functions consult the full owner, package, member, quote, and database-link identity; missing, ambiguous, stale, remote, or incomplete resolution is Unknown and fails closed. Share the profile and generation scoped resolver with .82 view, synonym, and policy proof work. Until such proof exists, never call a potentially callable identifier proven read-only.

Guard tests

- Direct SELECT of bare, package, schema-package, quoted, synonym, default-argument, and database-link zero-argument functions refuses before caller SQL evaluation.
- DML and CALL or PL/SQL spellings cannot lower the required authority.
- Real columns, aliases, record fields, and pseudocolumns remain usable only when positively resolved as data.
- Catalog errors, stale generations, replacement, synonym changes, overload changes, and current-schema changes invalidate or refuse.
- Live autonomous logging function: refused query leaves the log unchanged.
- Streaming and non-streaming read paths use the identical resolved verdict.
notes: PARTIAL FIX LANDED (this session): qualified paren-less callables (SELECT hr.dangerous_fn FROM dual, pkg.member) now FAIL CLOSED on the served DEFAULT_CLASSIFIER via a token-scope heuristic (unresolved_qualified_calls + query_scope_qualifiers, flag guard_unresolved_qualified_calls, wired on the served gate). RESIDUAL: an UNqualified bare zero-arg function (SELECT run_ddl FROM dual) is still lexically indistinguishable from a column and needs exact catalog identity -> RES-4. Keep open until RES-4 closes the residual.
close_reason: Exact served catalog resolution now distinguishes real columns from unqualified zero-argument functions and refuses functions before evaluation on ordinary and streaming paths. Live autonomous-transaction witness stayed at zero on XE18, XE21, and FREE23; focused live-feature clippy passed.

title: [QA100][P0][guard] Resolve SQL CALL targets before purity admission
description:
Finding

Oracle CALL target spellings are resolution-dependent. A two-part pkg.run name can denote a current-schema package or type member as well as a schema-qualified standalone routine, while bare names and synonyms depend on current schema and catalog state. The current SideEffectOracle accepts only ObjectRef with optional schema plus name and therefore cannot prove that a purity node is the routine Oracle will invoke.

Fresh verification

An independent completion review challenged the initial QA81 implementation that allowed CALL pkg.run when ObjectRef pkg.run returned ProvenReadOnly. Official Oracle CALL grammar and subprogram invocation rules permit standalone, packaged, type, schema-qualified, and synonym-resolved targets. The PlsqlSideEffectOracle graph lacks current-schema and object-kind context. A strongest-case AllProof test now confirms every CALL form remains Forbidden; no repo-local bead described exact CALL resolution.

Impact

A proof for an unrelated standalone function or package member could clear a different runtime target, allowing transitive DDL, ADMIN, autonomous, or external effects under READ_WRITE. This violates the profile ceiling and confirmation ladder.

Interim containment

QA81 forbids every explicit CALL even when the current purity oracle returns ProvenReadOnly. This bead is the only path to safely restore CALL admission.

Proposed fix

Add an active-profile and generation-scoped Oracle name resolver that returns a canonical owner, object kind, package or type, member, overload, quote semantics, synonym chain, and database-link status. Bind purity to that exact identity and invalidate proof on schema, synonym, overload, edition, or generation changes. Remote, ambiguous, stale, incomplete, or missing resolution remains Unknown and Forbidden.

Guard tests

Cover bare, schema, package, schema-package, type method, quoted, synonym, overload, default-argument, and database-link targets. Prove colliding schema and package names never share proof. Prove current-schema and synonym changes invalidate cached resolution. Verify argument expressions are independently resolved. Add a live pair of same-spelling routines where only one is read-only and show the wrong runtime target never executes.
notes: Still CONTAINED by bead .81/QA81 (every explicit CALL is Forbidden). Not a live fail-open. Safe restoration of CALL admission via exact ObjectIdentity is RES-5. Leave OPEN (tracks the restoration).
close_reason: Fresh verification confirms no live defect remains: QA81 already forbids every explicit CALL, including under an all-accepting two-field purity oracle. Exact identity is necessary but cannot prove arbitrary PL/SQL bodies/arguments pure in the engine-free binary, so blanket refusal is the correct safety design and is now documented.

title: [QA100][P1][streaming] Forward true streaming through MetricsDispatch
description:
Finding

MetricsDispatch implements ordinary dispatch, close, and surface-state forwarding, but does not override dispatch_stream. The ToolDispatch default silently calls ordinary dispatch and emits no incremental frames.

Fresh verification

Served HTTP enables MetricsDispatch in normal production wiring. K10 row-by-row streaming reaches this wrapper, so streaming=true is converted back into the buffered non-stream path before OracleDispatcher sees dispatch_stream. Tracker searches for MetricsDispatch and dispatch_stream found no duplicate; the closed K10 beads assume the wrapper preserves the stream contract.

Impact

True row-by-row SSE streaming is silently disabled on served HTTP whenever metrics are enabled, increasing latency and memory use and contradicting the advertised streaming behavior. Cancellation/backpressure coverage also exercises a different path than production.

Proposed fix

Override dispatch_stream in MetricsDispatch and forward the frame sender to the inner dispatcher while applying the same bounded metrics accounting used by ordinary dispatch. Keep dispatch_stream_start behavior delegated through the lane runtime. Do not duplicate query execution or buffer frames in the metrics layer.

Guard tests

Wrap a stream-aware recording dispatcher in MetricsDispatch, send multiple frames, and prove their order/content and terminal outcome are preserved. Assert exactly one duration/status observation. Add a served HTTP SSE regression with metrics enabled proving the first row frame arrives before final completion and cancellation reaches the lane.
notes: Fresh verification confirmed production HTTP dispatchers are wrapped by MetricsDispatch inside LaneRuntime, whose streaming command invokes ToolDispatch::dispatch_stream. Without an override, the trait default called buffered dispatch and emitted no frames. MetricsDispatch now forwards the exact ToolStreamSender and terminal outcome to the inner stream-aware dispatcher while sharing the same exactly-once status, blocked-label, and duration accounting as ordinary dispatch. Guards prove two ordered row frames are observable before terminal completion, buffered dispatch is never called, lane/subject metrics record exactly once, and mid-flight cancellation reaches the inner lane and records one cancelled outcome. Focused tests 2/2 and the full combined workspace gate passed: clippy -D warnings, all workspace tests/trybuild/integrations/goldens/docs, fmt, diff check, API lock, and cargo deny.
close_reason: Confirmed and fixed: MetricsDispatch now preserves true row streaming, cancellation, terminal outcomes, and exactly-once metrics.

title: [QA100][P1][quarantine] Never reuse uncertain pinned read sessions

True streaming already quarantines, while OraclePool correctly dirty-discards only the failed checkout. Impact: a protocol-uncertain session can serve later calls, violating the closed B1c never-reuse contract. Proposed fix: centralize ownership-aware uncertainty handling; quarantine retained pinned connections as UnknownDiscarded, but let pool-backed stateless reads rely on per-checkout dirty discard instead of poisoning the whole dispatcher. Guard tests: fail-once pinned raw and generated reads refuse the next call without DB I/O; pooled Cancelled discards only that checkout and a fresh read succeeds; deterministic ORA-00942 remains usable.

Uncertain errors quarantine retained primary sessions as UnknownDiscarded before reuse; distinct stateless pool workers rely on checkout dirty-discard and do not poison the active primary. Deterministic ORA-00942 remains reusable. Added four dispatch regressions covering pinned raw/generated refusal without second DB I/O, ordinary SQL reuse, and stateless isolation. Green: focused 4/4; workspace fmt and diff; workspace Clippy -D warnings; cargo deny; full workspace suite including 229 oraclemcp lib, 83 binary, 448 core, 318 DB, compile-fail, integration, golden, and doc tests.

Proposed fix: return Result<Option<OracleRow>, DbError>; degrade only proven ordinary privilege/query errors, propagate uncertain failures, and apply ownership-aware quarantine. Candidate profile failures must discard the candidate without poisoning the active session. Guard tests: Cancelled and ORA-03113 propagate; ORA-00942 degrades; mutation executes zero statements; uncertain switch candidate is never installed.

title: [QA100][P1][flashback] Quarantine failed AS-OF teardown
description: Finding: read_query_as_of discards DBMS_FLASHBACK.DISABLE failure whenever the read also failed and unconditionally ignores the final rollback result. Impact: a pinned session can be returned while flashback or stale transaction state remains active, contradicting the shipped always-torn-down contract. Proposed fix: preserve the primary diagnostic as context but make any disable or final rollback failure structural UnknownDiscarded/Quarantined so the physical session cannot be reused; cleanup stays freshly bounded. Guard tests: read-error plus disable-error quarantines; success plus rollback-error quarantines; successful disable and rollback preserve the original read result; subsequent use is refused.

The fix always evaluates both teardown operations; any DISABLE or rollback failure returns structural DbError::Quarantined(UnknownDiscarded) with the primary read outcome retained as context. The thin adapter now quarantines failed rollback/Flashback cleanup by dropping the physical driver connection and retaining a structural reason, so later ping/query cannot reuse it. Guards cover exact read-error preservation on clean teardown, read error plus DISABLE failure with rollback still attempted, successful read plus final rollback failure, and subsequent thin-session refusal. title: [QA100][P1][top-sql] Preserve uncertainty in historical source detection

Proposed fix: make the source resolver use uncertainty-preserving Result probes; only deterministic privilege or absence results may select fallback, while uncertain errors stop probing and reach ownership-aware quarantine. title: [QA100][P2][auth] Remove durable full-store writes from every bearer request
description:
Finding

Every successful service-owned client bearer authentication rewrites and fsyncs the entire clients.json file before the request reaches its per-principal rate limiter. Authentication is therefore a serialized durable-disk operation on the hot path, including for requests that are subsequently rejected with 429.

Evidence

- crates/oraclemcp-core/src/client_credentials.rs:335-386 holds the store mutex, validates the bearer, updates last_used_at and last_source_addr, then calls persist_locked for every valid request.
- persist_file at lines 455-505 pretty-serializes the complete client collection and calls FileStore::write_root_atomic.
- crates/oraclemcp-core/src/file_store.rs:271-293 creates a temporary file, writes all bytes, sync_all, renames it, then fsyncs the root directory.
- crates/oraclemcp-core/src/http/mod.rs:1353-1375 authenticates service client credentials; operator and MCP route flows call that before try_admit_http_request_rate at lines 1763-1772 and 5058/5109/5239 respectively.
- Defaults permit 600 requests per second with a 1200-request burst, but this cost occurs before that protection.
- Tests assert last-use metadata changes but do not bound write frequency, prove coalescing, or cover persistence failure after otherwise valid authentication.
- A full unlimited search of open, closed, and deferred beads found only the original credential-store and rate-limiter feature beads, not this interaction defect.

Impact

One valid noisy client can serialize all credential authentication behind full-file durable writes, amplify disk wear and latency as client count grows, and turn disk pressure or a transient write failure into 503 responses for every otherwise valid request. The advertised rate limiter cannot protect the expensive step because it runs later. This is an authenticated availability weakness and a normal-load scalability defect.

False-positive checks

Durably recording credential issuance, rotation, and revocation is intentional. Last-use telemetry does not need per-request durability to preserve authentication or immediate revocation semantics. Even multiple requests within the same timestamp second rewrite identical metadata, so this is not limited to genuine metadata changes.

Proposed fix

Keep bearer verification and revocation/generation reads synchronous and in-memory. Coalesce last-use/source metadata through a bounded asynchronous updater, such as at most once per client per minute, with an explicit shutdown flush and nonfatal telemetry-write policy. Where identity can be verified cheaply, apply the per-principal limiter before optional durable bookkeeping. Do not weaken immediate credential rotation/revocation persistence.

Guard tests

1. Count store writes: a large valid-request burst causes at most the documented coalesced number, including requests rejected by the limiter.
2. Concurrent authentication for one and many clients remains correct while writes are bounded and mutex hold time stays small.
3. A last-use telemetry persistence failure does not convert every valid credential request into 503 under the chosen fail-safe policy.
4. Rotation and revocation remain immediately durable and invalidate old credentials and active lanes.
5. Restart/shutdown tests document the permitted staleness of last-used metadata without exposing bearer values.
close_reason: Remove the durable full-store write from the bearer auth hot path. authenticate_bearer persisted last_used_at/last_source_addr via a full fsync+rename+dir-fsync on EVERY successful bearer auth, so an authenticated client hammering the endpoint forced an fsync per request (I/O DoS + flash-wear amplifier). Fix = coalesce the last-use write: should_persist_last_use() persists only when there is no prior timestamp (first use) or now has advanced >= LAST_USED_COALESCE_WINDOW_SECS (60s) past the stored one (a future stored ts from clock rewind also persists to correct it); otherwise the durable write is skipped. This bounds the durable write to at most one per minute per client, fully defusing the write-amplification regardless of request rate. Pure decision fn unit-tested with synthetic timestamps (no clock seam needed). NOTE: the bead also suggested reordering the rate-limit check before the durable write; that is subsumed by coalescing (an attacker can no longer force more than ~1 durable write/min/client no matter the ordering), so I did not restructure the http call sites — surfaced here rather than silently. Green: core client_credentials 10/0, fmt + clippy clean.

title: [QA100][P1][compile] Report partial persistent compile-session effects
description: Finding: compile_object_inner may successfully ALTER SESSION PLSQL_WARNINGS or PLSCOPE_SETTINGS, then receive a definite error on a later setup or compile statement and record plain Failed/write-intent Failed. Those earlier session changes persist despite rollback. Impact: audit and retry guidance claim no effect while the lane has changed policy. Proposed fix: track every completed sub-effect, restore prior session settings under fresh bounded cleanup when possible, and otherwise report a non-retryable partial persistent effect with truthful audit/intent state and quarantine if restoration is uncertain. Guard tests: first setup succeeds and second fails; no plain no-effect Failed is recorded, restoration is verified, and uncertain restoration prevents reuse.
close_reason: Confirmed against live Oracle: separate ALTER SESSION warning/PLScope setup persisted after a later definite compile error, while audit/write-intent reported plain Failed. Fixed at the root by emitting one unit-local ALTER ... COMPILE with explicit PLSQL_WARNINGS/PLSCOPE_SETTINGS clauses and REUSE SETTINGS, so surrounding session settings never change. VIEW rejects PL/SQL-only options. Guards cover one-statement builder shapes, package/type bodies, view refusal, exact preview/execute SQL, and a deterministic ORA-04043 path with exactly one DB effect, Pending-to-Failed audit, resolved FAILED intent, no quarantine, and reusable connection. Registry, README, API lock, and reviewed golden were updated. Full pinned fmt/clippy/workspace-test/API-lock/deny gate passed.

title: [QA100][P1][backstop] Clear read-only transactions before governed writes
description: Finding: ReadOnlyBackstop::disarm only flips an in-memory boolean. After SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY and a successful query, later elevation can route DML onto the same still-read-only Oracle transaction, yielding ORA-01456 even though the governed write is authorized. Impact: the operating ladder fails after ordinary reads and retry behavior is confusing; uncertain cleanup could also reuse bad state. Proposed fix: before the first governed write, perform a fresh bounded rollback that actually ends the read-only transaction, then disarm; quarantine on uncertain rollback and avoid auto-commit. Guard tests: read then elevate then DML succeeds under rollback-by-default; rollback failure prevents execute and reuse; live Oracle verifies transaction transition.
notes: Fresh verification confirmed Oracle SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY persists until COMMIT/ROLLBACK, so the previous boolean-only disarm left the pinned session in a real read-only transaction and authorized DML could fail with ORA-01456. The fix performs a fresh bounded cancellation-masked rollback at the exact post-gate/post-confirmation and pre-effect boundary; only success disarms. Failure leaves the tracker armed, records UnknownDiscarded quarantine, prevents the approved statement from reaching Oracle, and refuses later reuse. execute_sql covers oracle_execute/execute_approved/deploy/create-or-replace; compile and patch paths clear explicitly. Previews and classifier refusals do not clear the transaction. Guards cover read-elevate-DML success with rollback-by-default, DDL preview/confirmed compile ordering, rollback failure/no execute/quarantine/retry refusal, and refused writes preserving the arm. Focused 13/13 and the full workspace clippy/tests/trybuild/integrations/goldens/docs passed; fmt, diff check, API lock, cargo deny green.
close_reason: Confirmed and fixed: governed writes now end the real read-only transaction safely before effects, quarantining failed transitions.

title: [QA100][P1][lanes] Prevent creation after session lifecycle closure
description: Finding: stateful lane creation occurs outside the registry lock. Session DELETE, principal revocation, or shutdown can drain the current map while a request is still in factory preparation; that request may then insert and execute an orphan lane after lifecycle closure returned. The creation marker does not yet carry tombstones or cancellation. Impact: cancelled sessions can perform late DB work and leak a capacity/generation lease until shutdown. Proposed fix: unify creation and closure in a per-key lifecycle protocol; lifecycle operations tombstone/cancel in-progress creation, builder completion revalidates before insert, and all permits/prepared generations drop outside registry locks. Guard tests: barrier DELETE/revocation/shutdown during builder yields no execution, lane, or retained capacity; a later valid reinitialize can create exactly one fresh lane.
close_reason: Confirmed and fixed with a generation-token lifecycle protocol. Every resolution holds strong session-key, principal, and global generation tokens; DELETE, principal revocation, and shutdown invalidate the scoped generation while draining the registry under one Lifecycle-to-Registry lock order. Candidate spawn stays outside locks, then final generation validation and insertion are linearized; invalid candidates, stale lanes, prepared generations, and capacity permits release outside locks. Weak token entries self-prune and valid same-key reinitialization receives one fresh generation. Added deterministic barriers proving DELETE, principal close, and shutdown cannot install/execute in-flight candidates, plus exactly-one fresh same-key reinit. Green: focused check/tests, workspace fmt/diff, workspace Clippy, deny, and complete workspace test suite (448 core plus all crates/integrations/trybuild/docs).

title: [QA100][P1][cancellation] Wake queued lane replies when caller cancels
description: Finding: recv_lane_reply polls the reply oneshot and then observes caller cancellation only through a synchronous Cx checkpoint. It never registers a cancellation waker, so a caller cancelled while queued can remain parked until some unrelated reply wake; in the adverse interleaving the lane dequeues and enters the dispatcher, and the caller/test can deadlock waiting for work that should have been cancelled. Broad workspace evidence: caller_cancellation_while_queued_prevents_dispatcher_entry stalled beyond 70 seconds; isolated reruns passed, consistent with a lost-wake race. Deterministic proof design: poll once with unsignalled reply and a counting task Waker, cancel the Cx, assert the task is woken, then poll to Cancelled. Proposed fix: poll a never-initialized asupersync OnceCell::wait(cx) cancellation sentinel alongside the reply, with reply-first ordering so authoritative terminal truth still wins. Guard tests: cancellation wakes a parked receiver exactly once; second poll returns Cancelled; simultaneous ready reply still wins; queued command never enters dispatch.
close_reason: Confirmed lost-wake race: a queued caller could park without registering on Cx cancellation, and the lane could dequeue before the caller republished cancellation. Fixed reply waiting with a public OnceCell cancellation sentinel and reply-first terminal ordering; retained a source-Cx clone solely as a read-only queued cancellation witness while keeping all database/factory effects on the lane-owned Cx. Deterministic tests prove external cancellation wakes the parked receiver and a source-cancelled queued command never enters dispatch; cancellation family and 30-run stress passed. Full pinned fmt/clippy/workspace-test/deny gate passed.

title: [QA100][P1][guard] Admit valid PACKAGE BODY and TYPE BODY create/replace units
description: Fresh verification while falsifying QA101 found a distinct create/replace defect. Normal valid stored-unit bodies are inconsistently rejected by the default guard: a trivial PACKAGE BODY with an anonymous BEGIN may pass, but a legal named terminator END p or a body containing subprogram declarations fails as MultiStatement/Unbalanced; valid TYPE BODY is likewise refused. oracle_create_or_replace advertises and detects PACKAGE BODY and TYPE BODY, while oracle_patch_source already has a bespoke body-shape override, so this is an availability/contract bug rather than the safety policy. Proposed fix: centralize token-aware stored-unit shape analysis for PACKAGE BODY/TYPE BODY, preserve DDL flooring and every dynamic-side-effect/trailing-SQL fail-closed check, and remove path-specific shape divergence. Guard tests: representative package/type bodies with member procedures/functions and named END classify Destructive/DDL; preview mints a DDL confirmation and performs zero I/O; confirmed apply executes exactly once. Negative tests keep malformed nesting, extra END, trailing DROP/GRANT, EXECUTE IMMEDIATE/file/network/scheduler markers, and anonymous-block controls forbidden. Verify editionable/noneditionable, AUTHID, comments, schema-qualified/quoted names, and patch-source/create-or-replace parity.
close_reason: Verified valid package/type bodies and foreign call specifications were rejected by divergent shape handling. Centralized token-aware stored-unit analysis, removed the patch-only override, preserved DDL/dynamic/trailing-SQL fail-closed gates, and added preview/apply/refusal/parity coverage. Full pinned workspace gates pass.

title: [QA100][P1][query] Stream bounded pages before Vec row materialization
description: Fresh QA89 completion audit found that the new encoded row budget drops an oversized aggregate Value, but ordinary positional and named read paths still fetch max_rows+1 OracleRow values into a Vec before page accounting. One individual cell Value is also materialized before its encoded size is known; max_col_width can be unset. Thus emitted row payloads are bounded, but driver and per-cell transient memory can still exceed max_result_bytes substantially. Proposed fix: extend the owned row stream or a visitor interface to positional and named ordinary reads, serialize/account each row before fetching the next, stop at row and byte boundaries without skip/repeat, and add backend-aware bounded cell encoding so text/LOB/nested values cannot allocate beyond the remaining page budget. Preserve flashback teardown, cancellation quarantine, named binds, complex-value fallback, and byte-identical normal pages. Guard tests: first-row and later-row oversize, 5000 wide rows, one unbounded text cell, nested cursors/LOBs, exact boundary, named and positional binds, cancellation/backpressure, driver fallback, and a peak-memory assertion proving O(page byte cap plus one bounded cell), not O(max_rows times cell caps).
close_reason: Confirmed Vec materialization in ordinary positional/named reads. Added production one-row driver paging with immediate byte accounting, bounded expandable-cell materialization, cursor-safe resume, named-bind parity, fallback compatibility, and unit/live guard tests.

title: [QA100][P1][query/http] Enforce a whole MCP response byte budget
description: Fresh QA89 completion audit established that max_result_bytes is enforceable in oraclemcp-db only as the sum of compact row-object payloads. Columns, array separators, pagination metadata, sealed cursors, structured tool results, JSON-RPC or SSE framing, and replay-store cloning are added later and remain outside that cap. The registry is now truthful about this narrower law, but the original whole-response availability goal remains. Coordinate with open QA100 bead .52, which specifically bounds stateful replay retention. Proposed fix: define one core dispatch response-budget type with a documented minimum structural allowance; charge DB payload, metadata, cursor, tool envelope, negotiated MCP or SSE framing, and retained/replayed representation with checked arithmetic. Oversized results become a bounded typed error or resource reference before replay insertion; never advertise a cap smaller than the unavoidable error envelope. Guard tests cover exact/cap+1 pages, wide metadata, sealed cursors, JSON and SSE, stateful replay, stateless and stdio, nested data, concurrency/global accounting, and measured serialized bytes at the actual wire boundary.
close_reason: Enforce a whole-MCP-response byte budget. New crate::response_budget module: ResponseByteBudget charges the ACTUAL serialized wire bytes (serde_json::to_vec) of the finalized JSON-RPC response — envelope (payload embedded twice: fenced content[0].text + structuredContent), column metadata, cursor, JSON-RPC frame + reserved transport framing — before any transport writes it or the replay store retains it. In-budget -> passes through byte-identical; oversized (or non-serializable, or overflow) -> fail-closed to a bounded typed -32001 'response too large' error whose own size is proven <= OVERSIZED_RESPONSE_MAX_BYTES (giant request id dropped to null; ceiling clamped so it can never be below the error envelope it must emit; compile-time assert). Wired at every response boundary: stdio dispatch (server.rs:1222/1279) and both HTTP outcomes Ok+Err (http/mod.rs:6400/6402). Default ceiling 64 MiB sits above the legit ~50 MiB max page (25 MiB row cap embedded twice). 10 module unit tests + 168 lines of http tests. Green on main: core lib 570/0, full core suite 0 failed (golden HTTP unchanged), fmt+clippy clean.

title: [QA100][P1][plugin] Bound plugin helper descendant pipes and process trees
description:
Finding

The plugin runner repeats QA9: it waits only for the direct child and then unconditionally joins stdin/stdout/stderr workers. A plugin that exits successfully after spawning a descendant with inherited stdout or stderr can therefore exceed the advertised timeout indefinitely; timeout/error cleanup kills only the direct child and can leak descendants/readers.

Evidence

- crates/oraclemcp-core/src/plugin.rs:166-245 uses wait_timeout for the direct child followed by unconditional writer/stdout/stderr joins.
- QA9 fresh static fourth-instance audit found the identical successful-parent/pipe-inheriting-descendant control flow after fixing iam_token.
- Existing tests cover direct never-exit and large response/stdin deadlock, not successful parent plus inherited descendant pipe.

Impact

A configured plugin can wedge or exhaust the MCP process beyond its deadline and accumulate descendants/workers across calls.

Proposed fix

Reuse the reviewed command-group process group/Windows Job Object containment from QA9. Apply one end-to-end deadline to direct wait and every I/O worker, kill and reap the whole tree on every success/timeout/error exit, cap output, and preserve redacted typed errors.

Guard tests

- Successful parent with stdout-inheriting and stderr-inheriting descendants returns/fails within deadline and leaves no descendant.
- Repeated direct timeouts leave no process or reader growth.
- Existing finite, oversized, malformed, crash, and stdin-before-output cases remain green.
- POSIX and Windows cfg paths compile and use equivalent whole-tree ownership.
close_reason: Confirmed by fresh runtime reproduction: a 250ms invocation took 2.007s when a successful parent left either stdout or stderr inherited by a descendant. Fixed with command-group POSIX process-group/Windows Job containment, one wait-and-I/O deadline, whole-tree termination/direct-child reap on every exit, capped drains, and redacted errors. Added 10x inherited-pipe stress, 10 repeated timeout-tree leak checks, output-cap/redaction guards, and preserved all existing plugin tests; focused 14/14 tests and plugin-clean clippy passed.

title: [QA100][P2][admission] Add pre-authenticated remote control ingress
description: Residual after QA95: the shared listener can safely reserve pre-auth ingress for the default local operator and local doctor/readiness traffic because peer loopback is server-derived. It cannot guarantee reserved availability for an allow-listed remote OAuth operator: authority is learned only after request parsing, while hostile remote sockets can arrive before authentication. QA95 deliberately refuses remote pre-auth reserve rather than trusting a path/header/subject claim. Add a separately bounded control ingress whose privilege is established before general request parsing (for example a dedicated control listener with mandatory mTLS and allow-listed certificate identity, or an equivalent OS-authenticated channel). Keep the ordinary listener fail-closed. Guard tests must saturate ordinary workers with hostile remote peers, prove an allow-listed remote operator and readiness channel still enter, prove unauthenticated peers cannot occupy the control reserve, enforce absolute handshake/header deadlines, and prove total workers never exceed configured caps.
close_reason: Fresh-eyes confirmed QA95 deliberately leaves remote operator reserve unavailable. Added optional [http.control]/--control-listen as a second mandatory-mTLS listener with registered-and-operator-allowlisted certificate identity established before HTTP parsing; independent bounded pre-auth handshake and authenticated operator/doctor ledgers; absolute TLS/header/body deadlines; control-only route classification; shared graceful shutdown. Guards saturate hostile ordinary workers and control handshakes, prove remote operator/readiness entry, reject no-cert/unregistered/non-operator/MCP traffic, and lock caps/deadline release. Green: focused 2/2, core lib 617/617, config 117 + parity 5 + example, binary 120/120, strict core+binary all-target clippy.

title: [QA100][P2][secrets] Bound keyring helper time and output
description:
Finding

OS-keyring secret resolution invokes both the operator-selected ORACLEMCP_KEYRING_COMMAND and platform keyring helpers with std::process::Command::output, imposing neither a wall-clock deadline nor stdout/stderr size caps. A wedged helper can block startup or reconnect forever; a noisy helper can allocate unbounded memory.

Evidence

- crates/oraclemcp-auth/src/secrets.rs:225-265 selects the environment override or platform helper and funnels both through run_keyring_command.
- run_keyring_command calls Command::new(...).args(...).output() synchronously. output waits for process exit and buffers complete stdout and stderr into memory.
- Linux secret-tool and macOS security use that same path at lines 268-281.
- main resolves these references for database credentials and several security/operator secrets at main.rs:805, 1209, 1501, 2401, and 3914; database request timeouts do not bound a resolver that runs before connection.
- Keyring tests exercise parsing and an injected resolver seam, but no hanging, oversized-output, child-cleanup, or redaction behavior of the production command runner.
- A full unlimited Beads search found the original SecretResolver feature and onboarding references, but no keyring command deadline/output defect.

Impact

A locked GUI keyring, broken secret service, buggy platform helper, or misconfigured operator override can indefinitely wedge service startup, reconnect, configuration validation, or security-key initialization. Unbounded helper output can exhaust server memory. These failures occur on a trusted local integration seam, but they defeat service liveness and can be triggered repeatedly by normal recovery paths.

False-positive checks

Direct argv execution avoids shell injection and the helper is operator-configured; neither property bounds a legitimate executable that hangs, prompts, forks, or writes excessive data. The IAM token helper already documents and partially implements the need for deadlines and caps, confirming the expected local-command safety posture.

Proposed fix

Create one reusable bounded direct-command runner for secret and token helpers: closed stdin, one end-to-end wall deadline, independently capped stdout and stderr, process-group or platform-job cleanup, direct-child reap, descendant-safe output collection, and redacted typed errors. Keep argv direct and never include secret bytes in logs or errors.

Guard tests

1. A helper that sleeps or waits for stdin returns a typed timeout within a bounded margin.
2. stdout and stderr larger than their caps fail cleanly without excessive allocation.
3. A helper that exits after spawning a pipe-inheriting descendant cannot wedge joins and leaves no process/thread leak.
4. Normal one-line secret, empty output, invalid UTF-8, and nonzero exit have documented results.
5. Sentinel secret/output bytes never appear in Debug, Display, logs, or protocol errors.
6. Platform helper and ORACLEMCP_KEYRING_COMMAND both use the same hardened runner.
close_reason: Confirmed by fresh production-runner reproduction: direct sleep and successful parents with stdout- or stderr-inheriting descendants each took about 2.006-2.007s without any deadline. Hardened the single keyring runner used by the environment override and Linux/macOS adapters with closed stdin, direct argv, a five-second end-to-end deadline, POSIX process-group/Windows Job containment, whole-tree termination/direct-child reap on every exit, independently capped output, zeroized stdout, discarded stderr, typed failures, and redacted errors. Added hang, 10x inherited-pipe, cap, UTF-8/nonzero, redaction, stdin, and 10-retry process/worker-leak guards. Full auth 56/56, doctests, rustfmt, and all-target clippy -D warnings pass.

title: [QA100][P1][SIEM] Require confidential transport for audit shipping
description:
Finding

Audit SIEM shipping accepts an arbitrary plaintext http:// endpoint and sends both the configured secret authentication header and signed audit payload to it. No configuration or runtime boundary requires TLS for a remote host.

Evidence

- crates/oraclemcp-config/src/lib.rs:173-227 documents HTTP(S), stores the endpoint as an unchecked String, and validates only that a destination exists and auth options accompany an endpoint.
- crates/oraclemcp/src/main.rs:1490-1516 resolves siem_auth_header_ref to a secret and attaches its value verbatim to the forwarder for any endpoint scheme.
- crates/oraclemcp-core/src/audit_shipping.rs:84-181 clones the endpoint and headers into the outbound POST without a transport-security check. The body contains the signed audit record and, by design, may include SQL preview and subject/decision metadata.
- The only network test explicitly proves a plaintext loopback HTTP URL is accepted; there are no remote-HTTP rejection or secret-plus-HTTP tests.
- Documentation recommends HTTPS in examples but repeatedly calls the field HTTP(S), so this is accepted behavior rather than a parser accident.
- A full unlimited Beads search found no SIEM TLS or cleartext-transport task.

Impact

A plausible configuration typo or internal HTTP endpoint transmits the SIEM ingest token and privileged audit metadata in cleartext to network observers and intermediaries. Possession of the token may permit forged ingest or access to the SIEM endpoint; exposed audit previews and identities can reveal schema and operational activity. Protected profiles do not change this transport behavior.

False-positive checks

Shipping is operator-configured and off by default, but safe-by-default handling of secret material should reject an insecure remote destination rather than rely on a comment. Plaintext loopback can be useful for tests or a same-host proxy; it can be permitted under an explicit narrow rule without allowing remote cleartext. Signed records provide integrity, not confidentiality.

Proposed fix

Parse and validate the endpoint once. Require HTTPS for every non-loopback host and whenever a secret auth header is present. Permit loopback HTTP only under a documented local policy; if a broader insecure override is truly required, make it explicit, noisy, default-off, and forbidden for protected profiles. Do not follow redirects to a less secure scheme and validate the effective destination used by the HTTP client.

Guard tests

1. Remote http:// with and without siem_auth_header_ref is rejected by default.
2. https:// endpoints are accepted; malformed and unsupported schemes fail with actionable errors.
3. Loopback HTTP behavior is explicit and covered, including auth-header policy.
4. HTTPS-to-HTTP redirect or endpoint rewriting cannot downgrade the request.
5. Protected profiles cannot enable an insecure override.
6. Errors and logs include only the safe endpoint/reason and never the auth value or payload.
close_reason: Confirmed: remote plaintext and redirect downgrade could expose signed audit records and SIEM auth. Added validated HTTPS/literal-loopback policy, HTTPS-only auth headers, no-redirect runtime behavior, redacted diagnostics, docs, and regression tests.

title: [QA100][P1][audit] Move SIEM network delivery off the audit mutex
description:
Finding

Durable audit append holds the global chain-state mutex while the shipping decorator performs synchronous SIEM network POSTs. An unreachable or slow endpoint therefore adds up to the per-record network timeout to privileged actions and head-of-line blocks all other auditing, despite documentation saying shipping is off the request hot path and failures are nonfatal.

Evidence

- crates/oraclemcp-audit/src/sink.rs:604-650 locks Auditor state before sink.append and retains that lock across sink.flush for durable records. The lock is necessary for sequence/hash serialization, but its scope includes the entire decorated flush.
- crates/oraclemcp-audit/src/shipping.rs:221-240 fsyncs local storage and then synchronously calls forward_pending before returning.
- forward_pending at lines 197-219 loops over every pending record and calls each forwarder serially.
- crates/oraclemcp-core/src/audit_shipping.rs:99-181 builds a runtime and blocks on one HTTP POST with a five-second default timeout. Its comment at lines 136-139 incorrectly calls this off the request hot path.
- Production privileged paths call Auditor::append with durable=true synchronously, including dispatch/mod.rs:2661 and core query_execute.rs:248/271; they cannot execute until append returns.
- Existing shipping tests cover order and non-propagation of failures, not latency isolation, slow readers, concurrency, queue bounds, or restart delivery.
- A full unlimited Beads search found the original shipping feature and reactor fix but no network-under-audit-lock issue.

Impact

A slow, unreachable, or maliciously slow-reading SIEM can add roughly five seconds per durable audited action and serialize unrelated lanes behind the auditor mutex. A pending batch can multiply that delay. Because shipping errors are swallowed only after waiting, an optional fail-safe mirror becomes a service-wide availability dependency and can cause request pileups.

False-positive checks

Local fsync must remain synchronous and fail closed before privileged execution; moving that step would weaken the invariant. Remote shipping is explicitly a nonfatal mirror, so its network completion is not required before database execution. Forwarding outside only the shipping pending mutex is insufficient because the outer Auditor mutex remains held.

Proposed fix

Keep local append/fsync and chain-head advancement synchronous. After local durability, enqueue an immutable signed record to a bounded durable spool and let a dedicated supervised worker deliver in order with retry/backoff. Release the Auditor mutex before network I/O. Define overflow, shutdown, restart replay, observability, and destination-reconfiguration semantics; never silently discard without a durable local indicator.

Guard tests

1. A slow/unreachable forwarder does not materially delay local durable append or an audited action.
2. Concurrent audited lanes preserve a gap-free local chain while shipping is stalled.
3. Queue/spool is bounded, exposes depth/failures, and applies the documented overflow policy.
4. Restart replays undelivered records in sequence without duplicate local audit entries.
5. Multiple forwarders preserve per-destination order and isolate one slow destination.
6. Local append/fsync failure still fails closed before execute, proving the core safety invariant remains intact.
close_reason: Confirmed Auditor held its chain mutex through synchronous SIEM/WORM delivery. Fixed with per-destination bounded durable file spools and supervised ordered workers; local audit append/fsync remains synchronous fail-closed, external I/O is asynchronous and nonfatal. Added durable overflow indicators, exclusive spool ownership, restart recovery/order, destination binding, WORM replay idempotence, SIEM idempotency headers, observability, and shutdown persistence. Guards cover slow/unreachable isolation, concurrent gap-free local chain, bounded overflow, restart replay, multi-destination isolation, reconfiguration/ownership, worker panic retry, WORM tail dedupe, and local flush failure. Audit 123/123, core SIEM 7/7, focused spool 9/9, clippy/check/deny green.

title: [QA100][P2][audit] Harden audit files against symlinks and permissive modes
description:
Finding

The audit log, lock sidecar, and anchor temporary file are opened with ordinary path-following APIs and without enforced private file modes. In a shared or attacker-writable configured audit directory, preplanted symlinks can redirect writes or truncate an operator-writable target; under permissive umask/custom layouts, security records can also be created world-readable.

Evidence

- crates/oraclemcp-audit/src/sink.rs:100-141 opens <audit>.lock with create/read/write following symlinks, then after acquiring the fd lock calls set_len(0) and writes the PID. A symlink target is therefore truncated and replaced with PID text.
- FileAuditSink::open at sink.rs:230-248 follows an audit-path symlink and creates the log without an explicit Unix mode or a post-open ownership/type check.
- crates/oraclemcp-audit/src/anchor.rs:138-164 opens the fixed <audit>.anchor.tmp path with create(true), truncate(true), and no no-follow/create-new protection before rename. A preplanted symlink can be repeatedly truncated on durable appends.
- crates/oraclemcp/src/main.rs:1324-1338 uses create_dir_all for the audit parent and then opens the sink. Unlike FileStore, it does not enforce 0700 directories or 0600 files.
- The default audit path is computed under XDG state, but build_auditor runs before FileStore::open_default hardens the state root; read-only configurations with an explicit audit key may never open FileStore. Custom /var/log or WORM-style layouts remain entirely outside FileStore hardening.
- A full unlimited Beads search found prior audit locking/resume work but no symlink/no-follow or audit-mode issue.

Impact

A local user able to write the configured audit directory can cause startup or each durable anchor update to clobber another file writable by the oraclemcp account. An audit-path symlink can divert or corrupt the security record. Permissive modes can expose SQL previews, subject identifiers, outcomes, and operational metadata to other local users. Default private layout mitigates much of the steady-state exposure but does not make custom/shared paths safe.

False-positive checks

The attacker needs local directory-write access or an unsafe operator-selected layout; this is not a remote vulnerability. Advisory flock prevents two cooperating writers but does not prevent path redirection. Atomic rename protects the final anchor replacement, not the initial truncate of a symlinked fixed temporary path. Documentation tells operators to protect the log, but the safe-by-default sink should fail closed on unsafe filesystem objects.

Proposed fix

Centralize secure audit-path opening. Validate parent ownership/type/mode; reject symlink and non-regular targets with symlink_metadata plus post-open identity checks; use no-follow/openat-style APIs where supported. Create lock/data/temp files with 0600 and create_new, use unpredictable same-directory temp names for anchor replacement, fsync directories, and validate link count/owner according to the platform policy. Harden acceptable existing modes or fail with an actionable diagnostic.

Guard tests

1. Preplanted symlinks for the audit file, .lock, and .anchor.tmp cause fail-closed startup/update and leave target bytes unchanged.
2. FIFO, directory, device, and unexpected hard-link cases are rejected without blocking.
3. New audit, lock, anchor, and temporary files are 0600 and default directories are 0700 on Unix under umask 000 and 022.
4. Existing overly broad modes are hardened or rejected according to the documented policy.
5. Normal restart, lock contention, anchor update, and audit verify remain crash-durable and cross-platform.
6. Custom shared/WORM paths get an explicit ownership/mode diagnostic rather than silently weakening safety.
close_reason: Harden audit files vs symlinks + permissive modes, mirroring file_store.rs. sink.rs AuditLogLock::acquire + FileAuditSink::open used plain OpenOptions (followed symlinks, no mode); anchor.rs used a fixed <anchor>.tmp with create+truncate (preplanted symlink truncated on every durable update); main.rs build_auditor used plain create_dir_all. Added reject_unsafe_existing (symlink_metadata pre-check), harden_open_regular_file (post-open fstat identity + fchmod 0600, cfg(unix)), private openers (O_CREAT|O_EXCL, append, lock), unpredictable hidden same-dir anchor tmp created exclusively, and create_private_audit_dir (reject symlink/non-dir, 0700 create, harden existing broad dir). Tighten-only. 4 guard tests: symlinked log/lock fail closed + target intact, dir/fifo rejected, 0600-create + harden-existing. Green: oraclemcp-audit 142/0, oraclemcp lib 246/0 + cli 27/0, fmt + clippy (audit + oraclemcp) clean. Worktree-agent co-authored.

title: [QA100][P1][HTTP] Mark dashboard and MCP cookies Secure on TLS
description:
Finding

Both privileged dashboard-session cookies and stateful MCP-session cookies omit the Secure attribute even when the server is using native HTTPS. Cookies are host-scoped rather than port-scoped, so a later plaintext HTTP request to the same hostname can disclose them to another service or a network observer.

Evidence

- crates/oraclemcp-core/src/dashboard_auth.rs:431-434 always renders oraclemcp_dashboard_session with Path=/, Max-Age, HttpOnly, and SameSite=Strict, but no Secure.
- crates/oraclemcp-core/src/http/mod.rs:1575-1577 does the same for the stateful MCP cookie at Path=/mcp.
- The dashboard cookie is emitted by the pairing/login path at http/mod.rs:1875; the MCP cookie is emitted from sse_response at lines 5946-5961.
- Native TLS requests run through serve_https_until at lines 6101 onward but reuse the same HttpTransportConfig/response functions; no secure-transport bit reaches either cookie formatter.
- SameSite=Strict limits cross-site requests and HttpOnly blocks script reads, but neither prevents a browser from sending the cookie over plaintext HTTP to the same host. Browser cookies are not isolated by port.
- Existing tests assert HttpOnly/SameSite behavior but never assert Secure for HTTPS or define trusted reverse-proxy scheme handling.
- Independent HTTP review confirmed the path, and a full unlimited Beads search found no Secure-cookie task.

Impact

The dashboard cookie is a long-lived authenticated operator session and its session view yields CSRF/action tickets for guarded dashboard routes. If it is exposed through same-host plaintext navigation, subresources, a second local service, or network interception, an attacker can impersonate the operator within the remaining session policy. An exposed MCP session identifier can disclose or interfere with stateful transport state when combined with the applicable principal context.

False-positive checks

Loopback-only plaintext HTTP is an intentional supported mode, so unconditionally adding Secure would break local http:// browser use. The defect is that native HTTPS is not distinguished and therefore gets the weaker cookie too. Reverse-proxy termination cannot safely trust arbitrary X-Forwarded-Proto; it needs an explicit trusted-proxy/external-scheme contract.

Proposed fix

Carry an authenticated transport-security flag into cookie generation and automatically append Secure for native TLS. Add an explicit fail-closed external HTTPS/trusted-proxy setting for terminated TLS rather than trusting caller headers. Consider __Host- cookie names for dashboard sessions, which require Secure, Path=/, and no Domain. Document the constrained loopback plaintext exception and avoid setting privileged cookies remotely when the effective scheme is insecure.

Guard tests

1. Native HTTPS dashboard pairing and MCP initialize responses include Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite=Strict.
2. Loopback plaintext behavior is explicit and remains usable only within the intended policy.
3. Remote plaintext mode cannot mint privileged cookies.
4. Proxy mode ignores spoofed forwarding headers unless the peer/config is trusted and emits Secure only for a validated external HTTPS scheme.
5. Cookie names/path/domain satisfy __Host- rules if adopted, and logout/expiry uses matching attributes.
6. Browser-level regression verifies cookies minted on HTTPS are not sent to same-host HTTP.
close_reason: Confirmed TLS cookies omitted Secure. Added server-derived effective scheme, native rustls forcing, explicit trusted termination assertion with no forwarded-header trust, Secure dashboard/MCP cookies, loopback-only plaintext compatibility, remote plaintext suppression, matching DELETE expiry, docs and native/request regressions. Full workspace gates green with repo-local TMPDIR.

title: [QA100][P1][HTTP] Bound stateful session registries and reject failed initialize allocation
description:
Finding

Stateful HTTP initialization creates entries in two unbounded in-memory maps, with no global or per-principal session cap. The insertion predicate is only that the parsed request method string equals initialize, so even a JSON-RPC initialize that the server rejects receives and stores a live session.

Evidence

- crates/oraclemcp-core/src/http/mod.rs:901-981 defines HttpSessionStore as an unbounded HashMap; its idle reap scans the full map and collects/removes expired keys.
- HttpResultStore at lines 1002-1129 has a second unbounded session HashMap. Only events within one session are capped at 128.
- handle_mcp_post_exchange extracts method before dispatch and pre-mints a session id for every initialize at lines 5188-5229.
- After dispatch, every non-busy JSON-RPC response goes to sse_response. At lines 5919-5961 that function checks only method == initialize, not whether response.result is a successful initialize result, then inserts into both maps and sets a cookie/header.
- Repeated successful initializes also allocate indefinitely. They do not open database lanes, so the per-principal lane cap does not apply. The request limiter defaults to a 1200 burst and 600/s, while the idle TTL defaults to 900 seconds; sustained authorized traffic can retain roughly 540,000 empty sessions before expiry.
- Both HTTP and HTTPS listener loops invoke the O(n) idle scan about once per second.
- Existing tests cover once-per-session reinitialize, per-session event bounds, deletion, and idle expiry, but no failed-initialize allocation or aggregate session admission.
- Two independent reviewers confirmed the path; a full unlimited Beads scan found only closed worker/lane/session-binding features, not a pre-lane session-registry cap.

Impact

A valid but abusive client, or an unauthenticated client in an explicitly open deployment, can consume large amounts of memory and force repeated full-map CPU scans without using Oracle connections. As the registries grow, their mutex-protected operations and one-second reaper can degrade all stateful clients and eventually terminate the process through memory pressure.

False-positive checks

The 900-second TTL bounds retention time but not cardinality within the window. The 64 accepted-worker cap limits simultaneous connections, not sequential initialize requests. The 600/s rate limiter controls velocity but still permits a very high retained population and performs no aggregate admission. Per-session event capping does not cap empty sessions.

Proposed fix

Mint and insert a session only after validating a successful initialize response. Add coordinated global and per-principal session admission limits before allocation, returning the standard 429/AtCapacity envelope with retry guidance. Treat session and result-store entries as one lifecycle transaction so partial insertion cannot leak. Use an expiry structure whose steady-state reap cost is proportional to expirations rather than total population, and preserve operator/health reserve.

Guard tests

1. Parse errors, invalid jsonrpc, invalid initialize params, and other rejected initialize responses create no id, cookie, owner, or result-store entry.
2. The N+1 successful initialize for one principal and globally is rejected before allocation with stable retry metadata.
3. DELETE, credential revocation/rotation, idle TTL, and shutdown remove both store entries in lockstep and release capacity.
4. A request storm cannot exceed the configured map cardinality or cause unbounded reap work.
5. Caps are keyed only by server-derived bounded-cardinality principal identity and cannot starve operator/doctor reserve.
6. Valid initialization and protocol-version negotiation remain MCP-conformant.
close_reason: Confirmed rejected and repeated initialize requests allocated unbounded state.
